picks.reason: The repetition is real. Line 906 has two "the way" in one paragraph (the melon, then "the way it always had"), line 909 has a third, and "the way it always had" comes back word for word at line 1224. C fixes all of that. It keeps what the tail says, that her smile has always turned the room up, and says it the way a son talks about his mother. It changes the fewest words and keeps the meaning, which is the middle path. Her smile still does the work: the kitchen comes up a notch.
picks.problem_with_others: A and B make the same cut and only explain it differently. Dropping the tail loses the note that her smile has always done this. "Since he was six" is about her standard and "every night of his life" is about the ice cream, so neither carries it. That makes the line shorter by losing meaning, when a plain swap fixes the repeat.

picks.reason: The wording is Claude's (edit 66), and "He knew" is the narration glue that guide section 9 keeps out. Here it also makes a didn't-know/knew pair that mirrors itself. Joining the two sentences with "only that" is plain speech and keeps the broke man's math. It also reads better before the next sentence once row 11 changes. The reason is accurate, and it honestly flags that "more than he had" comes back at line 1000 in Chapter 12.
picks.problem_with_others: B gives the same wording with an accurate reason. A is picked only because it tells CT about the nearby repeat of "more than he had" at line 1000. C's "but it had to be more than he had" turns the fact into a guess and puts "had to be" next to "he had", which is clunky to say out loud.

picks.reason: "It wasn't a salary. It was an insurance policy" is the mirrored contrast CT has already rejected ("We've already established that we can do better than this"), and the wording is Claude's. "Insurance policy" is CT's own idea (edit 66: "that's where his insurance policy is"). The new line keeps CT's "his insurance policy" and the floor going out, and "the two spares" picks up Trent's "two spare robot arms" from the line above. "Would be" is still true when the policy fails to pay out in Chapter 15. Chapter 12 already covers the no-salary point ("getting paid in arms"), so nothing is lost. B's reason is accurate: "two of them" is at line 932 and "Two of them, Friday" is at line 998.
picks.problem_with_others: A and C give the same wording, so they lose only on their reasons. A puts the second "two of them" at line 997, but it is at line 998 (997 is "He worked at the cannery for three weeks on Trent's promise"). C's reason is fine but thinner, and B quotes CT's words exactly.

picks.reason: The original has two habits in one sentence ("looked at" and "for a while"). It also echoes line 903's "He looked at that one for a whole minute" a page earlier, and the chapter already has "a while" at 907 and 971. B swaps the time count for the action that makes him place it. The line before says the thermos read IRON DERBY "with most of the letters worn off", so reading what is left of the name sets up "Wait" and Gus grinning at the road. It is plain and concrete, and nothing happens that did not happen before.
picks.problem_with_others: A: "his eyes kept going back" is a stock line with his eyes as the subject, and it shows nothing new about the thermos. C: "Something about that thermos kept nagging at Elijah" is vague ("something about"). It also names the feeling instead of showing it and reads like a cliché, so the thermos acts only on paper.

picks.reason: "Didn't say anything" is the book's most-used silence beat (20 times, measured), and another one comes at line 832, about a page back. "Let it ride" is plain spoken idiom, and the verb does the kitchen-example work: the unanswered "Who's it work for?" rides along in the cab with them. That fits the next line, where Elijah moves on to "So what do you do with it?" It is also the move of the kind man who doesn't press, which Gus repeats when he takes the no about the show without pushing. The phrase appears nowhere else in the book.
